expertInsight: This exam is hard because it covers so many ways to connect systems: REST, SOAP, Bulk API, Platform Events, Change Data Capture, outbound messages, MuleSoft and Heroku Connect. The questions that slowed me down were the ones where the scenario was vague about timing. If the question doesn't say the user needs an answer right away, it usually isn't asking for a synchronous callout. Know the callout limits by heart (100 callouts per transaction, 120 seconds total). Also know what happens when a trigger hands work off to @future or Queueable. I got more questions on Connected Apps, OAuth and Canvas than I expected, so don't skip them.

whoIsThisFor.heading: Who should take the Salesforce Integration Architect exam?

personas.label: Senior Salesforce developers
personas.description: You build APIs and callouts and want to design complete integrations across Salesforce and other systems.

personas.label: Aspiring Salesforce architects
personas.description: You are developing architecture skills in integration as part of the broader System Architect path.

personas.label: Integration consultants
personas.description: You connect Salesforce with ERP, billing, and data platforms and want to validate your solution design skills.

examDifficulty.heading: How challenging is the Salesforce Integration Architect exam?
examDifficulty.summary: The exam requires both API knowledge and sound judgment about when to use direct connections, asynchronous messaging, batch processing, or middleware. Many questions describe a business need and ask you to balance timing, volume, reliability, and reuse.
bullets: 60 scored questions in 105 minutes, plus up to five unscored questions that do not count.
67% to pass, which is 41 correct answers out of 60.
Several integration patterns: Review REST, SOAP, Bulk API, Platform Events, Change Data Capture, outbound messages, and middleware.
Limits and failures matter: Understand callout limits, asynchronous Apex options, retries, and recovery patterns.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Practice drawing integrations from the scenario. Identify timing, data volume, direction, security, and failure handling before choosing a pattern. Aim for at least 80% on practice questions and be ready to explain the trade-offs.

examFormat.heading: Salesforce Integration Architect exam format
examFormat.intro: The exam is proctored online or at a test center. Questions focus on designing integrations for business requirements.
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Many questions describe data moving between Salesforce and another system. Determine whether the process must be synchronous or asynchronous, how much data is involved, and which system initiates the exchange.
bestWayToPass: Choose the pattern from the requirements: Ask whether a user needs an immediate answer, how much data moves, and what should happen if the target system fails.
Know API capabilities: Compare REST, SOAP, Bulk, Composite, Streaming, and data virtualization options.
Protect credentials: Use Named Credentials or the appropriate supported credential mechanism rather than putting secrets in code.
Use middleware when it helps: Consider system count, data mapping, reuse, governance, and operations before adding middleware.

introLead.text: Platform Integration Architect checks that you can design how Salesforce connects to other systems, from start to finish. It is one of the four exams you need for System Architect. See the

certificationCard.description: This exam covers Salesforce integration design, including API selection, asynchronous and event-driven patterns, middleware, security, reliability, and error recovery. The exam is 60 scored questions in 105 minutes, with a 67% pass mark, weighted towards Design Integration Solutions (28%) and Build Solution (23%).

blocks.heading: Integration Patterns
blocks.body: A request-and-reply pattern calls another system and waits for its response, such as validating an address during a save. Fire-and-forget sends a message without waiting for the receiver’s response; Platform Events and outbound messages can support this style. Batch synchronization moves larger data volumes on a schedule, often through Bulk API or an ETL tool. Data virtualization exposes external data without copying it into Salesforce, such as through Salesforce Connect and External Objects. Change notifications can update downstream systems or user interfaces when records change. Choose a pattern using response time, volume, system direction, and failure requirements.

blocks.heading: Salesforce APIs
blocks.body: REST is commonly used for lightweight reads and writes and uses HTTP resources. SOAP provides an XML-based contract, often described with WSDL. Bulk API 2.0 supports asynchronous processing of large data loads. Change Data Capture publishes record change events. Composite API groups related REST operations to reduce round trips and can support transactional behavior when configured. Consider API direction, volume, latency, payload, limits, and the capabilities of the other system when choosing an API.

blocks.heading: Reliability, Idempotency, and Recovery
blocks.body: Plan for timeouts, retries, duplicates, and downstream outages. Retry with increasing delays to avoid overwhelming an unavailable system. Idempotency means processing the same request again does not create duplicate effects; an external ID or request identifier can support this. A dead-letter queue holds messages that still fail and need review. A circuit breaker pauses calls after repeated failures and can queue work until the dependency recovers. Platform Events include replay identifiers so subscribers can resume within the retention window; outbound messages also retry failed delivery for a limited period.

blocks.heading: Platform Events and Change Data Capture
blocks.body: Platform Events carry messages that a publisher defines. Salesforce components or external systems can publish and subscribe, so the publisher need not know which consumers are listening. Change Data Capture (CDC) publishes changes to Salesforce records, including the type of change and changed fields. Subscribers can use supported streaming interfaces such as CometD or Pub/Sub API. Use Platform Events for business messages you define, CDC to communicate record changes, and outbound messages for supported declarative notifications.

blocks.heading: Middleware, MuleSoft, and API Governance
blocks.body: Direct connections may work for a small integration, but many systems and shared transformations can become difficult to manage. Middleware can route, transform, and govern exchanges. MuleSoft API-led connectivity organizes APIs into System, Process, and Experience layers. Exchange supports discovery and reuse of assets, while API management tools apply security and traffic policies. In Salesforce, Named Credentials keep endpoint and authentication configuration out of Apex source. External Services can use an OpenAPI description to make supported external operations available to Flow. Consider how to version and retire APIs without breaking existing consumers.

scenarioTips.h2: How to prepare for the Salesforce Integration Architect exam
scenarioTips.intro: Read each scenario for timing, volume, data direction, user interaction, security, and failure behavior. Those details narrow the integration pattern and API choices.

blocks.heading: Select an Integration Pattern
blocks.body: Use request-and-reply when a user needs an immediate response. Use asynchronous messaging or batch when the caller can continue without waiting. Consider data virtualization when external data should remain in its source system.

blocks.heading: Compare REST, SOAP, and Bulk API
blocks.body: REST supports common resource operations, SOAP provides an XML service contract, and Bulk API supports large asynchronous data jobs. Streaming and CDC communicate changes to subscribers.

blocks.heading: Distinguish Events from Record Changes
blocks.body: Use Platform Events for a message you define; use CDC to publish Salesforce record changes. Replay identifiers can help subscribers resume after an interruption within the retention period.

blocks.heading: Protect Credentials and Integrations
blocks.body: Keep credentials out of source code. Named Credentials manage endpoint and authentication configuration; use External Services when a supported API spec should be exposed to Flow.

blocks.heading: Plan for Scale and Outages
blocks.body: Use middleware when system count, transformations, reuse, or governance justify it. Include retry, idempotency, queueing, and circuit-breaker behavior for failure scenarios.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Related credentials for Salesforce integration architects
nextCertsAfter.intro: Continue with a Salesforce architecture, identity, or MuleSoft integration credential.

sampleQuestions.question: An address service must validate an address while a sales rep saves an Account. The rep needs the answer immediately. Which pattern fits?
options: Fire and forget using a Platform Event
Nightly batch synchronization
Synchronous request and reply callout
Data virtualization with External Objects
sampleQuestions.explanation: Request and reply lets Salesforce call the service and wait for its validation response before the user continues.
whyWrong: A fire-and-forget message does not return a response during the save.
A nightly batch cannot validate an address immediately.
Data virtualization exposes external data but does not provide this synchronous validation response.

sampleQuestions.question: A one-time migration must load eight million ERP orders into Salesforce. Which API is the best fit?
options: Bulk API 2.0
REST API with one request per record
Composite API for each order
Synchronous SOAP calls
sampleQuestions.explanation: Bulk API 2.0 supports asynchronous processing of large record volumes.
whyWrong: REST per-record calls add too much overhead for a migration of this size.
Composite API is for grouping related requests, not loading millions of rows.
Synchronous SOAP calls are a poor fit for this large asynchronous data load.

sampleQuestions.question: An Apex callout has a username and password hard-coded in its Authorization header. What should the architect recommend?
options: Store the password in a Custom Setting and read it in Apex
Use a Named Credential for endpoint and authentication configuration
Encrypt the password and put it in a Custom Label
Remove authentication and allow trusted IPs only
sampleQuestions.explanation: Named Credentials keep endpoint and authentication configuration outside the Apex source code.
whyWrong: Custom Settings are not the right place to store embedded credentials.
Named Credentials keep authentication configuration outside Apex source.
Custom Labels are not a protected credential store.

sampleQuestions.question: A warehouse needs changes to Opportunity records without custom code sending each update. Which Salesforce capability fits?
options: An Apex trigger that calls REST for every change
A scheduled report emailed to the warehouse
A custom Platform Event published from Flow
Change Data Capture for Opportunity
sampleQuestions.explanation: Change Data Capture publishes record changes for subscribed systems, including the changed fields.
whyWrong: This sends an individual callout for every update and adds custom code.
A scheduled report does not publish record changes to the warehouse.
A custom event requires the team to build the publishing logic.

sampleQuestions.question: An external billing system may send the same invoice again after a timeout. How can Salesforce avoid creating a duplicate invoice?
options: Disable retries in the billing system
Upsert by invoice-number external ID
Delete duplicates in a nightly cleanup job
Increase the API timeout to ten minutes
sampleQuestions.explanation: An external ID and upsert allow the same invoice identifier to update or match one Salesforce record instead of creating duplicates.
whyWrong: Disabling retries can lose an invoice when a temporary network failure occurs.
An external ID and upsert make repeat delivery idempotent.
A cleanup job only finds duplicates later and could remove valid data.

sampleQuestions.question: An external Platform Event subscriber was offline for six hours. How can it resume from its last processed event?
options: Events are lost whenever no subscriber is connected
Ask Salesforce Support to resend each event
Rebuild every missed record from a full nightly export
Reconnect using the replay ID of the last event processed
sampleQuestions.explanation: A subscriber can use its replay ID to request events from the point it last processed, subject to event retention.
whyWrong: Subscribers can replay events within the retention window.
Support does not manually resend each event.
A complete export is unnecessary when a replay position is available.

sampleQuestions.question: Salesforce must connect with an ERP, warehouse, billing system, and portal, and several teams will reuse customer and order data. What should the architect consider?
options: Middleware with reusable APIs
Direct point-to-point links between every system pair
Nightly CSV files on a shared FTP server
Separate Apex callouts built by each team
sampleQuestions.explanation: Middleware and reusable APIs can manage routing, transformations, and reuse across several systems and teams.
whyWrong: Reusable APIs and middleware help manage many systems and shared data.
Direct connections multiply as systems are added.
Shared files do not provide reusable APIs or timely integration.

sampleQuestions.question: A server-side integration must obtain Salesforce access for repeated REST calls with no user present. Which OAuth flow is designed for that pattern?
options: Web server authorization-code flow
User-agent flow
JWT bearer flow
Username-password flow
sampleQuestions.explanation: JWT bearer authenticates the server through a signed assertion and issues a token without asking a user to sign in.
whyWrong: Authorization-code flow requires user authorization.
User-agent flow is for public clients with interactive user access.
JWT bearer supports signed server-to-server access without a user.

sampleQuestions.question: A Queueable job makes one callout per record, and a transaction can contain 500 records. What is the main risk?
options: The trigger will run twice for every record
The transaction can exceed the 100-callout limit
Salesforce blocks all callouts from asynchronous Apex
Records will be saved without IDs
sampleQuestions.explanation: A transaction is limited to 100 callouts, so one per record for 500 records exceeds the limit.
whyWrong: A data load does not inherently make the trigger run twice per row.
A transaction can exceed the 100-callout limit with this workload.
Asynchronous Apex can make callouts when configured correctly.

sampleQuestions.question: Agents need current shipment data from a logistics system, and the data must not be copied into Salesforce. What should the architect consider?
options: Copy the data to a custom object every hour
Send changes by outbound message
Load shipment history with a nightly Bulk API job
Salesforce Connect with External Objects
sampleQuestions.explanation: Salesforce Connect and External Objects can expose external data without storing a copy in Salesforce.
whyWrong: Hourly replication means the data is still copied and may be stale.
Outbound messages do not expose current external shipment records.
A nightly load copies data and is not current during the day.

sampleQuestions.question: An admin needs to call an external currency API from Flow without writing Apex. An OpenAPI specification is available. What should they use?
options: External Services
Outbound messages
Canvas
Change Data Capture
sampleQuestions.explanation: External Services can use an OpenAPI description to expose supported external operations to Flow.
whyWrong: External Services can expose supported operations from an OpenAPI spec to Flow.
Outbound messages send Salesforce data out and do not call an API from Flow.
Canvas embeds an external app rather than exposing an API action to Flow.

sampleQuestions.question: When a Case closes, an outside help desk ticket should close without delaying the user. The team wants a declarative approach with retries. What fits?
options: A synchronous callout in a before-update trigger
A nightly batch job
An outbound message from a record-triggered Flow
A browser call from a Lightning component
sampleQuestions.explanation: An outbound message can send the notification asynchronously and retry delivery when the receiver is unavailable.
whyWrong: A synchronous trigger callout can hold up the user.
A nightly batch delays the close notification.
An outbound message can send asynchronously and retry delivery.

sampleQuestions.question: An external service is unavailable and requests are timing out. Salesforce keeps calling it and users are waiting. What design can help?
options: Increase the timeout to the maximum on every request
Retry each request immediately in a loop
Remove error handling to make calls fail faster
Use a circuit breaker and queue work during the outage
sampleQuestions.explanation: A circuit breaker pauses calls after repeated failures and can direct work to a queue until the service recovers.
whyWrong: A longer timeout can make users wait longer during an outage.
Immediate retries add load to the failing system.
Removing error handling does not queue work or prevent repeated calls.

sampleQuestions.question: An API v1 is used by five systems, and v2 changes field names. What is the safest migration plan?
options: Switch every consumer to v2 on the same day
Run v1 and v2 side by side and communicate a retirement date
Change v1 in place to return the new field names
Keep v1 forever and never release v2
sampleQuestions.explanation: Running both versions during a migration gives consumers time to move before the older version is retired.
whyWrong: A same-day switch may break consumers that have not migrated.
Parallel versions allow a planned transition before deprecation.
Changing v1 in place can break clients relying on its contract.

sampleQuestions.question: An external app must create an Account, Contact, and Opportunity together. If one fails, none should be saved. What should it use?
options: Three separate REST requests
Three Bulk API jobs
Composite API with allOrNone
Three outbound messages
sampleQuestions.explanation: Composite API can group related operations and use allOrNone behavior so the transaction succeeds or fails together.
whyWrong: Separate requests can leave partial records if a later call fails.
Bulk jobs are not intended for this small transactional set.
Composite API can group operations and use allOrNone behavior.
